verdict: real, known in part: the type is scala/bug#10908; the checker's cost on it is unreported
reran: cmd.sh on w4-int and w3-int: T.scala 2-4 s, -Ycheck:typer T.scala killed at 30 s, -Ycheck:all t498 killed at 30 s; on w3-base and 2.13.18 the same except -Ycheck:all t498 finishes in 3-4 s. Five thread dumps of w4-int -Ycheck:typer T.scala 4 s apart show different frames each time, all under TreeCheckers precheck.checkSymbolRefsRespectScope -> mkErrorMsg -> signature -> Symbol.defString; the run had printed 48 'Out of scope symbol reference' warnings after 22 s and 100 after 38 s (then the -Xmaxwarns cap hides the rest), so it is steady slow progress over a finite list, not a loop. A probe counts 1672 type parameters reported for T.f, and 3082 for t498's $anonfun$res, each message rendering an 834,460-character signature (0.2-0.6 s): about 5 to 20 minutes in all. Smaller shapes: if (b) List(1) else Vector(1) gets the same false reports (12 warnings, 2 s, 2.5 KB signature) on w4-int and w3-base; LazyList.empty vs Vector() has 1752 reports on a 685 KB type.
user_impact: Only -Ycheck users: compiler developers running partest or a debug build with -Ycheck on code whose inferred type is a large lub refinement (LazyList against a List or Vector, scala/bug#10908). Compiled code is unaffected. The false out-of-scope reports themselves appear for any lub refinement with polymorphic members, so -Ycheck output is noisy on ordinary collection code.
fixability: clear cut: in checkSymbolRefsRespectScope, treat type parameters bound inside the checked type (PolyType parameters of refinement members and type lambdas such as SeqFactory's CC) as bound, as retronym/scala PR 459 already does for existential quantifiers, and build the message once per tree with the signature truncated while printing rather than after rendering the full string. No compatibility cost; -Ycheck only. Belongs on the -Ycheck stack (PR 459 / 509) as one more false-report fix rather than a separate pull request.
regression: no: the out-of-scope check and its message format date from 2013 (288b12e48a, Paul Phillips) and the enormous type from the 2.13 collections; T.scala behaves the same on w3-base and 2.13.18. The -Ycheck:all difference on t498 is not a new hang: w3-base hangs with -Ycheck:uncurry alone exactly as the integration builds do with -Ycheck:all.
links: scala/bug#10908 (the lub of LazyList and List/Vector is an enormous refinement; wave three's inference track measured 828,788 characters for if (c) LazyList(1) else Nil, I measured 828,748). Retronym/scala PR 459 (Make -Ycheck re-typecheck a copy of the trees, in the integration build through 448) is the most likely reason -Ycheck:all now reaches the uncurry report; PR 419, 459 and 509 hold the earlier -Ycheck false-report fixes. WP1, WP2, WP4 are other -Ycheck findings with different causes.
note: The hunter's thread dump read the cause right but missed the root: the checker reports a false 'Out of scope symbol reference' for every type parameter bound inside the inferred refinement (B of updated, patch, zip, ..., A of type CC), and each report calls defString on the whole method signature before truncate(..., 80) cuts it to 80 characters; mk("tree", tree) renders the DefDef too. On the base, adding any earlier check phase (-Ycheck:typer, superaccessors, pickler, refchecks or patmat together with uncurry) makes the in-run uncurry check silent and the compile finish in 3-6 s, while running the same checker on the same uncurry trees after the run (a probe on w3-base) reports again; the uncurry trees and the lifted method's info are identical with and without the earlier check. So the base's quiet -Ycheck:all comes from state an earlier destructive check leaves behind, which I did not pin down; the integration build's non-destructive checking (PR 459, the only merged change that removes checker side effects; none of the merged PRs touches lub, existentials or Scope printing) removes that accident. This is not a finding against PR 459: it exposes an existing cost rather than adding one. The two programs have one cause.
